sm: Host Darren Rebehn talks with Indo-Pacific expert Andrew Harding about President Trump's trip to Asia, including the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. Harding says the meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, including a three-way session, were historic but produced little substance. The joint statement had four points: reform of the United Nations, more energy production and exports, protection of heads of state from prosecution by international courts, and agreement that a nuclear war cannot be won. Harding says no one expected a breakthrough and the countries are not aligned. He notes that optics favored the US and China, since Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac, while Putin was welcomed by a senior aide.

Harding says Xi and Trump sat together at dinner while Putin had his own table to the side, but all three were still treated as equals at the main meeting. He stresses that personal relationships should not be mistaken for strategic change, because the US and China remain competitors, as do the US and Russia, and China and Russia are partners but not natural allies. On nuclear weapons, he says the statement promises future dialogue, which is notable because China has resisted arms control while building more than a hundred warheads a year, possibly reaching about a thousand by 2030. He says Trump is right to raise the issue but also right not to trust adversaries, pointing out that New START has lapsed. He adds that Chinese state media reported Trump saying the US does not support Taiwanese independence, which he describes as unchanged US policy.

Harding says the trip should not be viewed only as a summit with Xi and Putin. He points to the first Quad leaders meeting of the president's second term, with agreements on a business forum, technology, cybersecurity, undersea cables and maritime security. In the Philippines, he says, there were deals on military financing, Boeing jets and technology investment worth billions of dollars, and a memorandum with Thailand on a trade agreement. He says this shows the US puts allies first. Looking ahead, he expects Xi to visit the US for the G20 in Miami in less than a month. A trade truce runs to January 2027, and he questions whether China is complying with the earlier Busan agreement on rare earths, setting up a possible trade showdown in early January.
